title: LDC exit set for 2029 as government eyes bonds and a new IMF deal
excerpt: The finance minister told Parliament graduation moves to 24 November 2029, and says a first sovereign bond could come within three months.

image.alt: Office towers and busy roads in central Dhaka seen from above

content:
Bangladesh will now leave the least developed country (LDC) group on 24 November 2029 instead of 24 November 2026, Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury told Parliament on 16 November. The UN General Assembly approved the three-year extension on 29 October, he said, in reply to a notice from reserved-seat MP Sultana Jasmine (UNB, via The Business Standard).

He said graduation will end duty-free market access and the TRIPS flexibilities that support the pharmaceutical industry, which meets 98 percent of domestic demand. A National Roadmap for Smooth, Sustainable and Irreversible LDC Graduation 2026-29 sets out five pillars, 21 action areas and 15 private-sector priorities. A monitoring committee he chairs is meant to meet monthly and has met twice.

To make up for shrinking concessional finance, the government is looking at its first sovereign bond and a Bangladesh-focused equity fund in Hong Kong. At a debt conference in Cox's Bazar organised with the Asian Development Bank, Khosru said a bond could be issued in New York or London "within two to three months", with Samurai, Panda and local Sukuk bonds to follow, The Daily Star reported. He said a new agreement with the International Monetary Fund is expected by February 2027, with talks in working groups due to finish in January or February, and that some conditions agreed by the previous, unelected government are hard to carry out quickly.

Key figures

  • Tk 1,27,520 crore budgeted for interest payments in 2026-27
  • Budget deficit target of 3.6 percent of GDP
  • $3.5 million over three years in a draft plan to boost trade competitiveness, presented at a commerce ministry meeting, with about $2.5 million proposed under the WTO's Enhanced Integrated Framework Phase Three for seven priority areas (bdnews24.com)

Why it matters

Graduation changes the terms on which donors lend and give to Bangladesh, and the extra three years give NGOs and their funders more time to plan for less grant money. A turn towards commercial bonds means more expensive debt, and the interest bill already takes money that could go to health, education and social protection.

What to watch

The size and cost of the first sovereign bond, the conditions in a new IMF programme, and whether the roadmap includes measures to protect social spending.
